abstract: Hybrid maize (Zea mays L.) parents are chosen within heterotic groups. Drought and heat stress are expected to become more frequent, but little is known about how they change the additive variance of each group and where in the genome it lies. We analyzed testcross grain yield from 62 Genomes to Fields environments, classified as low or high stress by climate. For 1,362 parents from three heterotic groups and two doubled-haploid families, we fitted a genomic model with group deviations and calculated local genomic estimated breeding values in 164-kb segments. In the heterotic groups, high stress reduced additive variance by 4057%, and the genetic correlation between conditions was 0.730.99. Within groups, the distribution of variance across the genome was similar between conditions (correlation 0.841.00), and genotype-by-environment interaction was spread over many low-variance segments. Genome-wide association detected 25 loci under low stress and 18 under high stress, none shared, but half or more lay in high-effect, high-variance segments that were nearly the same in both conditions. The best possible cross between the two heterotic pools exceeded the best evaluated hybrid by 105117%, a gap that depended on segment size, not on stress. With 25 founders, stacking the best segments reached 9495% of the pool potential, versus 5692% for selection on total breeding value, whose founders were more related. Founders chosen in one condition reached, in the other, 94100% of the potential of those chosen there. Local breeding values can guide the choice of donors and founders under both conditions.
